chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
The down payment is often the main obstacle to the first purchase. Good news: several tools, which can be combined, can help you build it up more quickly and with a real tax advantage. You still have to orchestrate them in the right order.

This guide dissects the minimum down payment, loan insurance, HBP, FHSA and family donation, with concrete examples adapted to Quebec.

2026 edition note: the ceilings (HBP, FHSA) and down payment thresholds are indexed or modified regularly. The amounts below are indicative - validate them with an advisor at the time of your project.

Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page to build YOUR down payment plan.

The down payment is often the main obstacle to the first purchase - but several tools, well combined, reduce it: FHSA, HBP, family donations. This guide explains how much you really need and how to put together your down payment intelligently.

The ceilings and thresholds (2026 edition) are evolving: this guide gives the logic, to be confirmed with your institution or your mortgage broker.

chapters.title: How much do you need?
chapters.objective: Calculate the minimum down payment and aim for a realistic goal.
chapters.html:
Calculate the minimum down payment and aim for a realistic objective.

The minimum down payment depends on the price (2026 edition, to be confirmed): 5% up to $500,000, 10% on the portion from $500,000 to $999,999, and 20% from $1,000,000.

  • Example at $400,000: 5% = $20,000.
  • Example at $650,000: $25,000 + $15,000 = $40,000.
  • Below 20%, loan insurance (CMHC, Sagen, Canada Guaranty) applies and is added to the loan.

Aiming for 20% avoids loan insurance, but waiting too long to get there also has a cost (paid rent, rising market). Balance is personal.

The key threshold is 20%: below, loan insurance (CMHC, Sagen, Canada Guaranty) is added to your financing, which increases the cost but allows you to buy sooner. Aim for a realistic goal rather than waiting years to avoid insurance - the market can rise faster than your savings.

Emilie's advice

Don't necessarily wait until you have 20%. Sometimes buying early with 5% and loan insurance is better than paying rent for two more years while prices rise. We do the math together.

chapters.title: FHSA: often the best starting point
chapters.objective: Use the most advantageous account for a first purchase.
chapters.html:
Use the most advantageous account for a first purchase.

The FHSA (tax-free savings account for the purchase of a first property) combines two advantages: your contributions are tax deductible (like an RRSP) and the withdrawal for a first purchase is tax-free (like a TFSA).

  • Limit of approximately $8,000 per year, up to $40,000 for life (to be confirmed).
  • Ideal to open early: even without contributing the maximum, this launches the account and your rights.
  • Combines with HBP for a first purchase.

The FHSA combines the best of the RRSP and the TFSA: tax-deductible contributions AND tax-free withdrawal for a first purchase, within annual and cumulative limits. It's often the very first account to open when saving for a first property - starting today, to start the meter.

Emilie's advice

Open a FHSA as soon as the purchase becomes a goal, even with a small amount: you accumulate contribution rights and prepare for a tax-free withdrawal on the big day.

chapters.title: The HBP: mobilize your RRSP
chapters.objective: Withdraw from your RRSP without immediate tax, then repay.
chapters.html:
Withdraw from your RRSP without immediate tax, then repay.

The Home Buyers' Plan (HBP) allows you to withdraw from your RRSP - up to $60,000 per person (amount recently increased, to be confirmed) - without immediate tax, for your down payment. You then repay this amount into your RRSP over 15 years.

  • An eligible couple can accumulate two HBPs.
  • Funds generally must have been in the RRSP for a certain period of time before withdrawal.
  • Annual reimbursement is mandatory; otherwise, the unreimbursed portion is added to your taxable income.

The HBP allows you to withdraw from your RRSP without immediate tax for the purchase, provided you repay over several years. A missed refund is added to your taxable income. FHSA and HBP can sometimes be combined - an arrangement to be validated with an advisor to maximize your down payment.

Emilie's advice

The HBP is a loan that you make to yourself: think about the annual repayment from the start. Well planned, it boosts your down payment without immediate tax bill.

chapters.title: Family donation and order of withdrawals
chapters.objective: Integrate a donation and orchestrate everything fiscally.
chapters.html:
Integrate a donation and orchestrate everything fiscally.

A donation from a close relative is accepted as a down payment by lenders, provided you provide a donation letter confirming that it is not a repayable loan. This is a subject in its own right (see the guide “Helping your child to buy”).

Order matters

FHSA, HBP, donation, unregistered savings: the order and timing of withdrawals have a real tax impact (deductions, tax refund, future contributions). A financial advisor or mortgage broker helps you sequence to maximize the benefit.

A donation from a close relative is accepted by lenders with a donation letter confirming that it is non-refundable. The order of withdrawals (FHSA, HBP, donations, savings) has a tax impact: plan it so as not to trigger unnecessary tax or weaken your financing file.

Emilie's advice

Before withdrawing anything, make a plan with an advisor. The correct FHSA/HBP/donation order can earn you a significant tax refund the following spring.

chapters.title: Beyond the down payment: the necessary cash
chapters.objective: Provide all the money required for the purchase.
chapters.html:
Provide all the money required for the purchase.

The down payment is not the only amount to raise. On the day of the transaction, other amounts are required:

  • Notary fees and disbursements.
  • Welcome tax (billed shortly after purchase).
  • Adjustments (taxes paid in advance by the seller).
  • Start-up costs and small emergency cushion.

Emptying your accounts to maximize your down payment means risking finding yourself without a margin from the first month.

Beyond the down payment, plan for closing costs (notary, welcome tax, adjustments) and an emergency cushion. Emptying your accounts to maximize the down payment means risking finding yourself without a margin from the first month of ownership.

Emilie's advice

Always keep a cushion after purchase. A property reserves its share of little surprises in the first months: it is better to have a slightly more modest down payment and an account that is breathing.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Calculate my minimum down payment and my objective.
  2. Open a FHSA if you have not already done so.

Within 30 days

  1. Meet with an advisor to sequence FHSA, HBP and donation.
  2. Document any family donation with a donation letter.

Then

  1. Validate the arrangement with a mortgage broker before making an offer.

To build my down payment

  1. Open a FHSA now to start the counter, even with small amounts.
  2. Have an advisor calculate the best FHSA/HBP/donation combination for my situation.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• Minimum down payment: 5% (up to $500k), 10% ($500k-$1M), 20% ($1M+), to be confirmed.
  • Loan insurance: required with 20% down payment (CMHC, Sagen, Canada Guaranty).
  • FHSA: deductible contribution + tax-free withdrawal for a first purchase (~$8,000/year, $40,000 for life).
  • HBP: RRSP withdrawal up to $60,000/person, repayable over 15 years (to be confirmed).
  • Donation letter: document confirming that a donation is not a repayable loan.
  • FHSA: account for first purchase - deductible contribution and tax-free withdrawal.
  • HBP: immediate tax-free RRSP withdrawal, to be repaid over several years.
  • Loan insurance: required under 20% down payment; is added to the financing.
  • Donation letter: document confirming that a family donation is not refundable.
  • Closing costs: notary, welcome tax, adjustments - in addition to the down payment.
